papers.title: Über die Bausteine der mathematischen Logik
papers.note: “On the building blocks of mathematical logic.” Presented in Göttingen in 1920. It introduces I, C (our K), T (our C), Z (our B) and S, and shows that S and C alone are enough. Combinatory logic starts here.

papers.title: Grundlagen der kombinatorischen Logik
papers.note: Curry's Göttingen dissertation independently rebuilds combinatory logic on B, C, K and W. W duplicates an argument, B composes, C swaps and K discards.

papers.title: Combinatory Logic, Volume I
papers.note: The standard reference on the subject. Among many others it defines Φ (the “formalizing” combinator, APL's fork) and Ψ (APL's ⍥ and BQN's ○).

papers.title: To Mock a Mockingbird and Other Logic Puzzles
papers.note: A book of puzzles set in an enchanted forest where every combinator is a bird: the Starling, Kestrel, Mockingbird, Thrush, Vireo, Dove and friends. The names stuck.

papers.title: A Programming Language
papers.note: The book whose title became the language's name: APL. It presents the notation first as mathematics and only later as a programming language.

papers.title: Notation as a Tool of Thought
papers.venue: Communications of the ACM 23(8), 444–465 · Turing Award Lecture
papers.note: Iverson's case that good notation makes you think better. Composing primitives such as +/ and × into bigger ideas is the heart of the lecture.

papers.title: A Dictionary of APL
papers.note: A rethink of APL's operators. Commute ⍨ appears: f⍨ ⍵ is ⍵ f ⍵ (the Warbler W), and ⍺ f⍨ ⍵ is ⍵ f ⍺ (the Cardinal C).

papers.authors: Kenneth E. Iverson & Eugene E. McDonnell
papers.title: Phrasal Forms
papers.venue: APL89 Conference Proceedings · APL Quote Quad 19(4)
papers.note: Introduces hooks and forks. (f g h) ⍵ is (f ⍵) g (h ⍵), which is Curry's Φ, and the hook (f g) ⍵ is ⍵ f (g ⍵), which is Schönfinkel's S. J adopted both, and Dyalog added trains in 2014.

papers.title: Dyalog APL 18.0
papers.note: Version 18.0 gave APL named operators for two more birds: f⍤g (atop, the Blackbird B₁ when used dyadically) and f⍥g (over, Curry's Ψ).

papers.title: BQN: finally, an APL for your flying saucer
papers.note: A modern array language that is open about its combinators. ∘ atop, ○ over, ⊸ before, ⟜ after and ˜ self/swap are each a single combinator, and trains work as in APL.

papers.title: Combinatory Logic and Combinators in Array Languages
papers.venue: ARRAY 2022 · ACM SIGPLAN Workshop on Libraries, Languages and Compilers for Array Programming
papers.note: Lines up the birds against APL, J and BQN, showing that tacit array programming is combinatory logic written in glyphs.

papers.title: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought
papers.note: The algebra of logic: and, or and not as operations you can calculate with. Every gate in this world is Boole's.

papers.title: A Set of Five Independent Postulates for Boolean Algebras, with Application to Logical Constants
papers.venue: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 14(4), 481–488
papers.note: Shows that a single operation, the “stroke” (not-and), is enough for all of Boolean algebra. Schönfinkel opens his 1924 paper by doing the same trick for logic, then for functions.

papers.title: A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits
papers.note: Shannon's master's thesis: Boolean algebra describes switching circuits, so circuits can be designed by calculation. Adders included.

papers.title: The Calculi of Lambda-Conversion
papers.venue: Annals of Mathematics Studies 6, Princeton University Press
papers.note: Data as functions: a boolean is something that chooses between two things, a number is something that repeats. True is K, false is KI.

papers.title: The Elements of Computing Systems
papers.note: Build a whole computer, and then Tetris on it, starting from a single NAND gate. Not, And, Or, Xor, Mux, then adders, an ALU, memory and a CPU.

levels.title: first flight
levels.blurb: Build something that ignores its first argument and returns the second.

levels.title: the idiot bird
levels.blurb: I x = x. Schönfinkel showed it isn't primitive at all.

levels.title: S K I
levels.blurb: Your first word. Two letters are free; one you have to make.

levels.title: composition
levels.blurb: B x y z = x (y z). Feed z through y, then through x.

levels.title: mirror, mirror
levels.blurb: M x = x x. A bird that sings its own song back to itself.

levels.title: turnabout
levels.blurb: T x y = y x. Hand x to whoever comes next.

levels.title: the cardinal
levels.blurb: C x y z = x z y. Swap the last two arguments.

levels.title: say it twice
levels.blurb: W x y = x y y. Duplicate an argument.
levels.hint: C S I — or S S (S K) with only Schönfinkel's birds.

levels.title: pairs
levels.blurb: V x y z = z x y. Hold two values until a selector arrives.

levels.title: B C K W
levels.blurb: Curry's basis, spelled out from Schönfinkel's.
APL's tacks are Kestrels: ⍺ ⊣ ⍵ is ⍺, ⍺ ⊢ ⍵ is ⍵.

levels.title: double it +⍨
levels.blurb: f⍨ ⍵ is ⍵ f ⍵: commute used monadically is the Warbler. +⍨ doubles.

levels.title: swap it -⍨
levels.blurb: ⍺ f⍨ ⍵ is ⍵ f ⍺: commute used dyadically is the Cardinal.

levels.title: atop ⍤
levels.blurb: ⍺ (f⍤g) ⍵ = f (⍺ g ⍵). The Blackbird composes after a dyad.

levels.title: sum of squares
levels.blurb: +/×⍨ ⍵: square each with ×⍨, then sum with +/. Two birds, one pipeline.

levels.title: the fork
levels.blurb: (f g h) ⍵ = (f ⍵) g (h ⍵). Iverson's fork is Curry's Phoenix Φ.

levels.title: avg ← +/ ÷ ≢
levels.blurb: The most famous train: sum divided by count.

levels.title: range ⌈/-⌊/
levels.blurb: Largest minus smallest, as a fork: (⌈/ ⍵) - (⌊/ ⍵).

levels.title: palindrome? ≡∘⌽
levels.blurb: A hook: does ⍵ match its reverse? (f g) ⍵ = ⍵ f (g ⍵) is the Starling.

levels.title: over ⍥
levels.blurb: ⍺ (f⍥g) ⍵ = (g ⍺) f (g ⍵). Curry's Ψ pre-processes both sides.

levels.title: ⍺ (f g h) ⍵
levels.blurb: The dyadic fork, Φ₁. Two phoenixes and a bluebird.
(⍺+⍵)×(⍺-⍵) as a dyadic train. Feed the Pheasant three functions.

levels.title: after ⟜
levels.blurb: 𝔽⟜𝔾 𝕩 is 𝕩 𝔽 (𝔾 𝕩). ∾⟜⌽ joins a list to its reverse. Another Starling.

levels.title: before ⊸
levels.blurb: 𝔽⊸𝔾 𝕩 is (𝔽 𝕩) 𝔾 𝕩: the mirror image of after. Call it Σ and build it.

levels.title: palindrome? ⌽⊸≡
levels.blurb: BQN's palindrome test: reverse first, then match against the original.

levels.title: the dove
levels.blurb: D x y z w = x y (z w): leave the left argument alone, transform the right.

levels.title: 𝕨 ∾⟜⌽ 𝕩
levels.blurb: Called dyadically, 𝕨 𝔽⟜𝔾 𝕩 is 𝕨 𝔽 (𝔾 𝕩): a Dove, once a Cardinal moves 𝔾 into its slot.

levels.title: before, dyadic
levels.blurb: 𝕨 𝔽⊸𝔾 𝕩 is (𝔽 𝕨) 𝔾 𝕩: transform only the left argument. Call it Δ.

levels.title: 𝕨 ⌽⊸∾ 𝕩
levels.blurb: Reverse the left list, then join: (⌽ 𝕨) ∾ 𝕩.

levels.title: same length? =○≠
levels.blurb: 𝕨 𝔽○𝔾 𝕩 is (𝔾 𝕨) 𝔽 (𝔾 𝕩). Over is Ψ in BQN too.

levels.title: 2-train ¬=
levels.blurb: 𝕨 (𝔽 𝔾) 𝕩 is 𝔽 (𝕨 𝔾 𝕩). “Not equal” as an atop train.
The average again, in BQN: sum-fold +´ divided by length ≠.

levels.title: true, false
levels.blurb: Church's booleans choose: true picks the first option, false the second. The bins try each on 1 and 0.

levels.title: not
levels.blurb: Not swaps the two options. You already know a bird that swaps.

levels.title: and
levels.blurb: p and q: if p then q, else p (which is false anyway).

levels.title: or
levels.blurb: p or q: if p then p (which is true), else q.

levels.title: if-then-else
levels.blurb: if c then a else b. With Church booleans the condition already does the choosing…

levels.title: exactly one
levels.blurb: Xor: true when exactly one input is true.

levels.title: Sheffer's stroke
levels.blurb: Not-and: false only when both are true. From this one gate, everything.

levels.title: Not from Nand
levels.blurb: nand2tetris chip #1: Not(in) = Nand(in, in). Feed one wire to both inputs.

levels.title: And from Nand
levels.blurb: And(a, b) = Not(Nand(a, b)). Compose after a two-input chip: the Blackbird.

levels.title: Or from Nand
levels.blurb: Or(a, b) = Nand(Not a, Not b). Pre-process both inputs the same way: that's Psi.

levels.title: Xor
levels.blurb: Xor(a, b) = And(Or(a, b), Nand(a, b)). A dyadic fork of the chips you've built.

levels.title: Mux
levels.blurb: Mux(a, b, sel): sel ? b : a. In hardware it's gates; with Church booleans it's just wiring.

levels.title: HalfAdder
levels.blurb: Your first chip with two outputs: sum = a ⊻ b, carry = a ∧ b.

levels.title: FullAdder
levels.blurb: Add three bits: sum is a ⊻ b ⊻ c, carry is the majority vote. Chain these and you have an ALU's adder.

code: -- the function Applicative: (f <*> g) x = f x (g x)
S.note: S feeds the same argument to both functions.
BQN's after ⟜, used monadically, is S.

K.note: const is K: keep the first argument, ignore the second.
Every callback that ignores its argument is a K.

KI.note: (a, b) => b is the Kite: keep the second.

W.note: join for functions duplicates the argument: W.

T.note: (&) is the Thrush; F# and Elixir spell it |>.

code: const pair = a => b => f => f(a)(b)
const fst = p => p(a => b => a)
V.note: The Vireo holds two values until a selector arrives.

B₁.note: The Blackbird composes after a two-argument function.

Φ.note: liftA2 on functions is the Phoenix: the monadic fork.

Ψ.note: on is Psi: pre-process both arguments.

Σ.note: Bind for functions is Σ: (f >>= k) x = k (f x) x.

D.note: Dyadic after: transform only the right argument.

Δ.note: Left-to-right composition, as in BQN's dyadic before.

⊤.note: A boolean is a choice: cond ? a : b is cond(a)(b).

code: const F = a => b => b  // the Kite
const not = p => a => b => p(b)(a)
~.note: Not is the Cardinal: swap the options.

∧.note: S C I, or S S K.

code: unsigned sum = a ^ b, carry = a & b;  // half adder
⊻.note: Xor is the sum bit of an adder.

⊼.note: The first chip in nand2tetris: Not from Nand, i.e. W ⊼.
